slides.title: TCP Connection Establishment
slides.body: TCP Connection Establishment

slides.title: TCP
slides.body:
Connection-Oriented
Both sides agree on starting Sequence Numbers — so data can be tracked in order
Both sides negotiate MSS (Maximum Segment Size) and Window Size — so each side knows how much data the other can handle

slides.title: TCP
slides.body:
Connection-Oriented
Both sides confirm the path works in both directions — sending and receiving are both functional

slides.title: TCP
slides.body:
All three of these happen inside a single process called the 3-Way Handshake
The TCP 3-Way Handshake is a process used by the Transmission Control Protocol (TCP) to establish a reliable connection between a client and a server prior to data transfer
Connection-Oriented

slides.title: A Connection Must Be Set Up Before Any Data Flows
slides.body: Analogy

slides.title: TCP 3-Way Handshake
slides.body:
Step 1 — SYN (Client → Server)
Step 1
The client is the one that starts the connection. The very first step is called SYN
The client sends a TCP segment with the SYN flag set to 1
The client picks a random number as its Initial Sequence Number (ISN) — for example, ISN = 100
This segment also carries the client’s MSS and Window Size

slides.title: TCP 3-Way Handshake
slides.body:
Step 1 — SYN (Client → Server)
Step 1
The client is the one that starts the connection. The very first step is called SYN
Message conveyed: “I want to connect. My starting sequence number is 100.”
After sending this, the client enters the SYN_SENT state — it is waiting for a response from the server

slides.title: TCP 3-Way Handshake
slides.body:
Step 1 — SYN (Client → Server)
The SYN flag counts as 1 byte in the sequence space even though it carries no application data. This matters in Step 2

slides.title: TCP 3-Way Handshake
slides.body:
Step 2 — SYN-ACK (Server → Client)
Step 2
The server receives the SYN from the client and responds. This response is called SYN-ACK
The server sends a segment with both SYN and ACK flags set
ACK Number = 101 (client’s ISN + 1) — this tells the client: “I received your byte 100. Now send me byte 101.”
The SYN flag counts as 1 byte — that is why the ACK number is ISN + 1 and not ISN itself

slides.title: TCP 3-Way Handshake
slides.body:
Step 2 — SYN-ACK (Server → Client)
Step 2
The server receives the SYN from the client and responds. This response is called SYN-ACK
The server picks its own random ISN — for example, ISN = 300
The server also sends its own MSS and Window Size in this segment
Message conveyed: “Connection accepted. Got your byte 100. My starting sequence number is 300.”
After sending this, the server enters the SYN_RECEIVED state

slides.title: TCP 3-Way Handshake
slides.body:
Step 3 — ACK (Client → Server)
Step 3
The client receives the SYN-ACK from the server and sends the final confirmation. This is the ACK

slides.title: TCP 3-Way Handshake
slides.body:
Step 3 — ACK (Client → Server)
Step 3
Connection is now fully open. Data can flow in both directions
The client receives the SYN-ACK from the server and sends the final confirmation. This is the ACK

slides.body:
Analogy
Yes , I can hear you loud and clear. Let us begin the meeting 
The caller says

slides.title: SYN Flood Attack
slides.body:
Consequence of 3-Way Handshake
When a server receives a SYN, it sends SYN-ACK and enters SYN_RECEIVED state
The server allocates memory and a connection entry, waiting for the final ACK
In a SYN Flood Attack, an attacker sends thousands of SYN packets with fake source IP addresses — and never sends the final ACK
The 3-way handshake has a well-known vulnerability called the SYN Flood Attack
How the Attack Works:

slides.title: SYN Flood Attack
slides.body:
Consequence of 3-Way Handshake
The server’s SYN queue fills up with half-open connections that will never complete
Real or authorized clients cannot connect — the server has no capacity left
This is a Denial of Service (DoS) attack
The 3-way handshake has a well-known vulnerability called the SYN Flood Attack
How the Attack Works:

slides.title: SYN Flood Attack
slides.body:
Direct
Real IP used. Easy to detect and block
Spoofed
Fake source IP on each packet. Harder to trace
Distributed (DDoS)
Uses a botnet. Nearly untraceable

slides.title: SYN Flood Attack
slides.body:
SYN Cookies
The server does not allocate memory on receiving a SYN. Instead it encodes connection information into the SYN-ACK as a cryptographic cookie. Memory is only allocated when a valid final ACK arrives with the correct cookie

Why 4 Steps Are Needed?
TCP uses 3 steps to open a connection
Connection setup
It uses 4 steps because TCP is full-duplex
Connection close
Each direction (Client → Server and Server → Client) must close separately
Reason
One side sends FIN, the other ACKs, then sends its FIN, which is finally ACKed

slides.title: TCP Connection Termination
slides.body:
Types of TCP Connection Release
TCP supports two types of connection releases like most connection-oriented transport protocols:
1
Abrupt Release
2
Graceful Release

slides.title: 1. Abrupt Connection Release
slides.body:
Closing Without 4-Way Teardown
The 4-way teardown is the graceful way to close a TCP connection. But TCP also supports an immediate forced close using the RST (Reset) flag

slides.title: 1. Abrupt Connection Release
slides.body:
Closing Without 4-Way Teardown
What is an Abrupt Connection Release?

slides.title: 1. Abrupt Connection Release
slides.body:
When does TCP send RST?
SYN arrives on a port with no listening service
Segment received for a non-existent connection (wrong IP/port)
Invalid sequence number causes the connection to go out of sync
Firewall or application forcibly terminates the connection
During handshake: Client detects invalid SYN-ACK (ACK ≠ ISN) and sends RST

slides.title: 2. Graceful Connection Release
slides.body:
Closing Using 4-Way Teardown
The 4-way teardown is the standard method to gracefully close a TCP connection. It ensures both sides finish sending data before the connection is closed
